class_name: Amphetamine-type monoamine releasers (TAAR1 + reverse transport at DAT/NET/SERT + VMAT2 reverse transport)
shared_mechanism: Amphetamine-type stimulants act on three converging substrates: (1) they are TAAR1 full agonists, with TAAR1 activation desensitising DAT via PKA/PKC and slowing dopamine neuron firing; (2) they are substrates for DAT/NET/SERT (depending on substituent pattern), entering the cytosol and causing reverse transport ('non-exocytotic release') by reversing the Na+/Cl- electrochemical gradient the transporters normally use; (3) inside the cytosol they are weak bases that collapse the proton gradient across vesicular VMAT2, displacing monoamines from synaptic vesicles into the cytosol where they can be reverse-transported out. The relative ratio of DAT:NET:SERT substrate activity is set by ring substituents — unsubstituted/N-methyl/2-fluoro favour DA+NE, 4-halogen shifts toward SERT, 4-methylthio/4-methoxy make the compound SERT-dominant. Rothman & Baumann's synaptosomal release-assay EC50 values (PMID 11071707, PMID 18307294) are the canonical reference.
shared_pk_summary: Most amphetamines are well absorbed orally (F = 70–100%), have small-to-moderate Vd (3–6 L/kg), low protein binding (15–40%), and are eliminated by a combination of CYP2D6 hydroxylation (para-hydroxylation, then COMT/SULT), N-demethylation (CYP2D6/CYP3A4), deamination (FMO3, DBH), and direct renal excretion of unchanged drug — which is pH-dependent because the protonated amine is a tertiary base (pKa ~9.9). Acidic urine increases renal clearance (t1/2 ~7 h); alkaline urine reduces it (t1/2 >20 h). Typical half-life of d-amphetamine in adults is 9–11 h; l-amphetamine is 11–14 h; d-methamphetamine 9–12 h. The α-methyl group is what protects amphetamines from MAO degradation (versus phenethylamine itself, t1/2 ~30 s).
shared_safety: The classic acute hazards are (1) hyperthermia (multifactorial: sympathomimetic vasoconstriction limits heat dissipation, 5-HT release activates 5-HT2A-mediated thermogenesis, mitochondrial uncoupling); (2) sympathetic crisis (HTN, tachycardia, MI, stroke, aortic dissection); (3) serotonin syndrome with serotonergic releasers especially combined with MAOIs or SSRIs; (4) for 4-halogenated and 4-thio/methoxy compounds (4-MTA, PMA, 4-CA, 4-BA) — selective serotonergic axonal neurotoxicity (Fuller PMID 1196472) and 5-HT2B-mediated cardiac valvulopathy / pulmonary hypertension (Rothman/Setola, PMID 11104741, PMID 12649293). PMA/PMMA are uniquely dangerous because they combine SERT release with MAO-A inhibition (IC50 300–600 nM and 1700 nM respectively, Reyes-Parada DOI:10.3389/fphar.2019.01590) producing delayed-onset hyperthermia and serotonin syndrome (peak 4–6 h after dose rather than 1–2 h, leading to repeat dosing). Long-term — chronic high-dose methamphetamine causes DAT/SERT terminal damage detectable by PET (McCann PMID 9504281). hERG is generally not the primary cardiotoxicity mechanism for this class (in contrast to cocaine analogues). 5-HT2B is the main valve risk; fenfluramine's metabolite norfenfluramine has Ki 11–52 nM at 5-HT2B (Rothman PMID 11104741) which is why fen-phen caused valvulopathy while phen-only did not (phentermine has no 5-HT2B activity).
sar_summary: Core SAR axes for amphetamine class: (1) α-methyl is essential for oral activity (protects from MAO; bare PEA t1/2 ~30 s) and for switching from PEA's primarily MAO-substrate behaviour to monoamine release. (2) N-methyl (→ methamphetamine) increases lipophilicity, BBB penetration, and DA:NE selectivity, and adds σ1 activity. (3) N-ethyl/N-propyl progressively reduce DA release while sparing 5-HT release, biasing the profile toward entactogen. (4) Ring substitution at the 4-position controls SERT engagement: 4-F is intermediate (DA>5-HT, EC50 200 vs 730 nM, Nagai PMID 17223101), 4-Cl is fully SERT-shifted and neurotoxic, 4-Br is similar to 4-Cl, 4-I likewise; 4-methyl gives p-toluidine analogues with SERT shift; 4-methylthio (4-MTA) and 4-methoxy (PMA) are SERT-dominant and add MAO-A inhibition. (5) 2-halogen retains DA selectivity (2-FA EC50 DA ~33 nM, SERT >10 µM — Wee PMID 15914673). (6) 3,4-methylenedioxy makes entactogens (MDMA family — covered elsewhere). (7) β-hydroxyl (→ ephedrine, norephedrine, cathinone family) reduces lipophilicity and CNS penetration ~10×, weakens DA release more than NE release, eliminates TAAR1 efficacy. (8) Beta-keto (→ cathinones) similarly reduces CNS penetration but is metabolised to β-hydroxy. (9) Oxazoline ring (→ aminorex family) gives long-duration releasers with 5-HT2B liability (aminorex caused PPH epidemic 1965–1972). (10) Para-methoxy specifically gives PMA — slow-onset, MAOI-active, deadly (DOI:10.1038/s41573-019-0049-9).

name: Amphetamine

binding.tissue_or_cell: HEK293 transiently expressing hTAAR1, cAMP readout
binding.notes: Bunzow et al. 2001 — original TAAR1 (then TA1) cloning paper; racemic amphetamine listed as full agonist with EC50 ~1.8 µM

functional.notes: Rothman 2001 Synapse — d-amphetamine, EC50 24.8 nM DA release
Rothman 2001 — d-amphetamine, EC50 7.07 nM NE release; ~3.5× more potent at NET than DAT
Rothman 2001 — d-amphetamine, very weak SERT releaser (~250× weaker than at DAT)

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Amphetamine enters DA terminals as a DAT substrate, activates cytosolic TAAR1, which signals through Gαs to elevate cAMP/PKA and through Gαq/Ca²+, both of which phosphorylate DAT at N-terminal serines (Ser7, Ser12, Ser53), promoting reverse transport. PKC activation also internalises DAT. Inside terminals, amphetamine collapses VMAT2 proton gradient (it is a weak base, accumulates in vesicles) and as α-MPT inhibitor / direct vesicle disruptor, dumps DA into cytosol which is then reverse-transported.

neuroimaging.finding: 0.3 mg/kg oral d-amphetamine reduces striatal [11C]raclopride binding by ~5–15%, corresponding to ~50–150% increase in extracellular DA; magnitude correlates with novelty-seeking scores and subjective 'wanting'

routes.notes: Markowitz & Patrick 2017 — d-amphetamine t1/2 9–11 h, l-amphetamine 11–14 h, Tmax IR 2.5–3.5 h, XR 5.3–8.2 h; protein binding 16–20%

metabolism.notes: Highly pH-dependent: 1–75% urinary recovery of unchanged drug; acidic urine clears faster

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 poor metabolisers show modestly reduced 4-hydroxylation but main clearance is renal — clinical impact is small. CYP2D6 inhibitors (paroxetine, fluoxetine, bupropion, quinidine) prolong amphetamine effects.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Negligible direct binding; serotonergic effects are via SERT release

data_gaps_remaining: Direct human σ1 binding data for racemic amphetamine
notes: The 'amphetamine' record in the user database is racemic. In clinical formulations the salt is usually d-isomer (Dexedrine) or 3:1 d/l mixture (Adderall). Pharmacological data above are for d-amphetamine — l-amphetamine has a separate record and is dramatically weaker at DAT but only slightly weaker at NET.

name: Dextroamphetamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See class context: TAAR1 → PKA/PKC → DAT phosphorylation → reverse transport; VMAT2 collapse dumps vesicular DA into cytosol.

neuroimaging.finding: Striatal DA release proportional to plasma d-amphetamine 1–3 h post-dose; healthy adults show ~10% raclopride displacement at 0.3 mg/kg

routes.notes: IR formulation Tmax 2.5–3.5 h; XR 5.3–8.2 h; t1/2 9–11 h adults, 6–8 h children

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: ion-trapping of protonated amine in urine
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Increases renal clearance, shortens t1/2 to ~7 h
Reduces clearance, prolongs t1/2 to >20 h

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: inhibition of monoamine catabolism + concurrent DA/NE release
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Hypertensive crisis, hyperthermia, fatal serotonin syndrome — absolute contraindication

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Minor; clearance is renal-dominant. Co-administered CYP2D6 inhibitors prolong effects more than genetic PM status alone.

notes: Dextroamphetamine is the more clinically used enantiomer; ~3–4× more potent than l-amphetamine on a per-mg basis at DAT, ~1.3× at NET. Adderall is a 3:1 d:l salt mixture intended to provide longer duration (l-amph t1/2 longer).

name: Dexedrine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Identical to dextroamphetamine — Dexedrine is the sulfate salt brand.

notes: Dexedrine is a brand name for d-amphetamine sulfate; pharmacology identical to Dextroamphetamine record.

name: (R)-amphetamine

functional.notes: Forsyth 2012; l-amph EC50 ~28 nM at DA — only slightly weaker than d-amph

l-amphetamine has the highest NE:DA selectivity ratio of any amphetamine (~3:1), and dose proportional NE release correlates better with the subjective 'rush' than DA release does (Rothman 2001 PMID 11071707)

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: l-amph has substantially weaker effect on DAT phosphorylation and DA release relative to d-amph but nearly equivalent NE release; explains why Adderall (3:1 d:l) is 'smoother' than pure d-amph (Dexedrine) — extra NE without proportional DA spike.

routes.notes: l-amph t1/2 11.7–15.2 h (longer than d-amph 9–11 h); accounts for tail of Adderall effect

notes: The R-(-)-enantiomer. Has the longest half-life of the amphetamine enantiomers. Selectively releases NE > DA >> 5-HT.

name: Adderall

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Adderall is a 3:1 (d):(l) amphetamine mixture of four salts: amph aspartate monohydrate (25%), amph sulfate (25%, both racemic), d-amph saccharate (25%), d-amph sulfate (25%) — yielding 75% d-amph / 25% l-amph by free base.

routes.notes: IR: Tmax ~3 h, t1/2 9–14 h (composite of d and l); XR (bead capsule, 50% IR + 50% delayed) extends Tmax to ~7 h, total clinical effect ~10–12 h; Mydayis is triple-bead, effect ~16 h

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: raises gastric pH, accelerates dissolution of XR coating
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Earlier Tmax, blunted second peak with Adderall XR
Modest increase in AUC and prolonged effect

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: Same as parent amphetamine — minor effect from CYP2D6 PM status

notes: Brand-name 3:1 d:l amphetamine. Pharmacology is the weighted combination of d- and l-amphetamine records.

name: Methamphetamine

binding.notes: Nichols/Nguyen — micromolar σ1 affinity; activation implicated in methamphetamine-induced neuroinflammation and dopaminergic neurotoxicity

functional.notes: d-meth EC50 8.5–24.5 nM (range across labs); ~3× more DA-potent than d-amphetamine
5-HT release EC50 ~1 µM — modest but non-trivial, accounts for some 'rush' euphoria distinguishing meth from amph
l-meth ~50× weaker than d-meth at DAT. This is the form released as metabolite of selegiline.
Only ~2× weaker than d-meth at NET; this is why l-meth (Vicks Vapor Inhaler) has decongestant action despite minimal CNS stimulation

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Methamphetamine adds two features to amphetamine pharmacology: (1) σ1 agonism, which through chaperone effects on D1, BiP/GRP78, and microglial NF-κB drives chronic-use neurotoxicity (Nguyen Pharmacol Rev 2017, doi:10.1124/pr.116.012799); (2) the N-methyl group increases lipophilicity, raising brain:plasma ratio and intracellular accumulation in DA terminals. Reactive oxygen species from cytosolic DA auto-oxidation are the proximate cause of DAT terminal degeneration (McCann 1998 PMID 9504281).

neuroimaging.finding: Chronic high-dose meth users show 24% lower striatal DAT density that persists ≥3 years after cessation

metabolism.notes: ~15% of meth dose appears as amphetamine in urine; useful forensic marker

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PMs show slightly higher meth plasma exposure and lower amphetamine metabolite; small clinical effect.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Vesicular DA depletion — substrate of contributing to cytosolic DA → ROS → terminal neurotoxicity

notes: Listed entry is racemic; clinical/illicit material is overwhelmingly d-meth. d-meth is ~3× more DA-potent than d-amphetamine; this and the σ1 component drive its higher abuse potential and chronic neurotoxicity profile.

name: D-methamphetamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See Methamphetamine record.

notes: The clinical and illicit form. See Methamphetamine record for full data.

name: L-methamphetamine

functional.notes: ~50× weaker than d-meth at DAT; this is why Vicks Vapor Inhaler (l-meth) has minimal CNS stimulation despite being structurally identical to street meth
Only ~2× weaker than d-meth — drives the decongestant/vasoconstrictor action

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Predominantly peripheral sympathomimetic via NE release; weak central DA action limits abuse potential.

routes.notes: OTC Vicks Vapor Inhaler contains 50 mg l-meth; produces detectable urinary meth (and amphetamine from N-demethylation) with no CNS effect — common forensic confound

notes: Also a metabolite of selegiline (deprenyl) at therapeutic doses — explains some of selegiline's amphetamine-like effects.

name: DL-methamphetamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Racemic mixture — pharmacology is the weighted average of d- and l-meth records.

notes: Racemic form. See D-methamphetamine and L-methamphetamine records.

name: 4-Fluoroamphetamine

binding.notes: Weak 5-HT2B partial agonism — concerning for chronic use but in low-μM range

functional.notes: Nagai 2007 — 4-FA is intermediate, releases DA at ~200 nM
4-FA shows meaningful 5-HT release (~4× weaker than DA) — accounts for empathogenic effects users describe; profile is between amphetamine and MDMA

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Intermediate between amphetamine and MDMA — DA release dominant but enough SERT engagement to produce empathogenic component.

routes.notes: de Sousa Fernandes Perna et al. — single 100–150 mg oral doses in healthy volunteers, t1/2 ~11 h, Tmax ~2 h

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Theoretical valvulopathy risk with chronic use — low-μM partial agonist, but exposure rarely reaches that range at typical recreational doses

notes: 4-FA is the canonical 'intermediate' fluoroamphetamine. Several Dutch case reports of cardiac events and cerebral haemorrhage at recreational doses.

name: 4-fa

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See 4-Fluoroamphetamine record (duplicate entry in source DB).

notes: Duplicate of 4-Fluoroamphetamine entry. See that record for full data.

name: 2-Fluoroamphetamine

functional.notes: Wee 2005 J Pharmacol Exp Ther — 2-FA is DA-selective releaser, similar potency profile to d-amphetamine with weaker SERT effect than 4-FA
EC50 >10 µM — essentially no SERT release; cleaner DA-selective profile than 4-FA

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Pure amphetamine-like DA-NE release — the 2-fluoro substitution does NOT shift toward SERT (unlike 4-fluoro).

notes: Ortho-fluoro is the 'safest' fluoroamphetamine regiochemically — DA-selective like amphetamine, without the 4-halogen shift toward serotonergic neurotoxicity.

name: 2-fa

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See 2-Fluoroamphetamine record.

notes: Duplicate of 2-Fluoroamphetamine. See that record.

name: 3-Fluoroamphetamine

functional.notes: Wee 2005 / Negus PAL-353 series — 3-FA potent DA releaser, similar to amphetamine
Weak SERT releaser — intermediate between 2-FA and 4-FA

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Behaviour close to methamphetamine in DA/NE release; meta-fluoro is a 'minimal-shift' substituent.

routes.notes: Jiang 2020 — t1/2 in rats ~90 min, comparable to amphetamine. Limited human data.

notes: 3-FA has stronger half-life-shortening effect (similar to amphetamine) than 4-FA — users report shorter duration.

name: 3-fa

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See 3-Fluoroamphetamine record.

notes: Duplicate of 3-Fluoroamphetamine.

name: 4-fma

functional.notes: Rickli 2015 — 4-FMA between 4-FA and methamphetamine in profile

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-methyl + para-fluoro pattern; SERT-shift weaker than 4-FA due to N-methyl reducing 5-HT efficacy.

notes: Less serotonergic than 4-FA, more amphetamine-like — limited published data.

name: 2-fma

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: 2-FMA is methamphetamine analogue with ortho-fluoro — predicted DA-selective, similar to 2-FA but with N-methyl boost; no published EC50 values.

notes: Popular UK research chemical, very limited literature.

name: 3-fma

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Predicted intermediate; no published data.

notes: Research chemical; no published literature.

name: 2-fea

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-ethyl shifts toward entactogen profile; ortho-fluoro keeps DA component intact. No published EC50 values.

notes: Research chemical, very limited data.

name: 2-Fluoroethamphetamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Duplicate of 2-fea entry.

notes: See 2-fea record.

name: 3-Fluoroethamphetamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-ethyl + meta-fluoro — predicted DA-SERT releaser similar to MDA in profile; no published EC50.

notes: Research chemical; very limited data.

name: 4-fea

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Predicted SERT-shifted (para-halogen + N-ethyl gives MDMA-like profile); no published EC50.

notes: Research chemical; no published literature.

name: 4-Fluoroethamphetamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Duplicate of 4-fea record.

notes: See 4-fea record.

name: 4-Chloroamphetamine

functional.notes: Fuller 1992 — PCA is the canonical highly selective SERT releaser

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Massive 5-HT release → MAO-A inhibition (IC50 1.9–4 µM) → serotonin syndrome → selective serotonergic axonal degeneration via cytosolic 5-HT auto-oxidation. Mechanism of long-term neurotoxicity still debated (toxic metabolite vs ROS).

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Adds to serotonin syndrome risk when combined with SERT release

data_gaps_remaining: No human clinical PK — research-only compound used in preclinical neurotoxicity models
notes: PCA is the prototype serotonergic neurotoxin amphetamine. Standard tool for inducing selective 5-HT axonal lesions in animals. NOT for human use.

name: 4-Chloromethamphetamine

functional.notes: Saha 2017 — similar to PCA, potent SERT releaser; N-methyl boosts NET activity

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Like PCA but with NET component from N-methyl. Equally neurotoxic to 5-HT terminals.

notes: Research chemical. Highly neurotoxic. Same risk profile as PCA.

name: 4-Bromoamphetamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Like PCA — para-bromo shifts to SERT-dominant releaser with serotonergic axonal neurotoxicity demonstrated in rats; depletes brain 5-HT ≥1 week (Fuller 1975 PMID 1196472).

data_gaps_remaining: No published EC50 release values; profile inferred from PCA homology and rat neurotoxicity data
notes: Same SERT-dominant + neurotoxic + MAOI profile as PCA. Not for human use.

name: 4-Methylthioamphetamine

functional.notes: Huang et al. — 4-MTA is potent SERT releaser, similar to PCA
Weak DA release — SERT-dominant

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: SERT-dominant release + MAO-A inhibition (IC50 250 nM) is the classic 'PMA-like' lethal combination. Hyperthermic serotonin syndrome with delayed onset. 4-MTA additionally has 5-HT2A agonism.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Severe serotonin syndrome + hyperthermia; multiple deaths attributed to 4-MTA + co-ingestion with serotonergics

notes: 4-MTA was marketed as 'flatliners' in the UK 1999–2001 and caused multiple fatal serotonin syndrome cases. The combination of SERT release + MAO-A inhibition is the lethal mechanism. Notably 4-MTA does NOT cause MDMA-like axonal neurotoxicity in rats despite equipotent 5-HT release — suggests neurotoxicity is not purely a function of SERT release magnitude.

name: 4-mta

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See 4-Methylthioamphetamine record.

notes: Duplicate of 4-Methylthioamphetamine.

name: Para-Methoxyamphetamine

functional.notes: Potent SERT releaser; combined with MAO-A inhibition this is the killing mechanism

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: SERT release + MAO-A inhibition (IC50 300–600 nM) → massive cytosolic 5-HT accumulation → serotonin syndrome with malignant hyperthermia. Onset is delayed (4–6 h) compared to MDMA (~1 h), causing users to redose thinking they got bad ecstasy.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Lethal serotonin syndrome with hyperthermia and delayed onset

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PMs have markedly impaired O-demethylation and clear PMA more slowly → higher risk of fatal toxicity. Multiple PMA deaths linked to PM genotype.

notes: PMA is the canonical 'fake MDMA' killer compound. Often sold as ecstasy. Delayed onset → redosing → fatal hyperthermia. CYP2D6 PMs are at multiplied risk.

name: Pma

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See Para-Methoxyamphetamine record.

notes: Duplicate of Para-Methoxyamphetamine.

name: Fenfluramine

binding.notes: Rothman/Setola 2000 — parent fenfluramine has weak 5-HT2B; the danger is its metabolite norfenfluramine

functional.notes: Potent SERT releaser — basis for anorectic effect
Essentially inactive at DAT

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Acute: SERT release → anorexia, satiety. Chronic: metabolite norfenfluramine accumulates → 5-HT2B-mediated mitogenesis on cardiac valves → fibrous valvular thickening (mitral and aortic), pulmonary hypertension. Now reformulated for Dravet syndrome (Fintepla) at much lower doses, with REMS for echocardiography. Anticonvulsant action likely involves σ1 modulation (Sourbron 2017 doi:10.1111/epi.13691).

routes.notes: Caccia 1986 — fenfluramine t1/2 13–30 h (mean ~19 h depending on enantiomer); active metabolite norfenfluramine t1/2 1.5–2× longer (~30 h), accumulates with chronic dosing

metabolism.notes: Norfenfluramine is 400× more 5-HT2B-active than parent (Ki 52 nM vs 4134 nM); also has 5-HT2C activity (Ki 557 nM)

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: additive monoamine release; phentermine has no 5-HT2B activity (fen alone was the valve culprit)
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Synergistic weight loss; valvulopathy/PPH driven by fen/norfen, not phen. 'Phen-fen' withdrawn 1997.
Reduces 5-HT2B exposure — potentially safer in PMs

pharmacogenetics.phenotype_effects: CYP2D6 PMs may have less norfenfluramine formation → potentially less valvulopathy risk but variable. UMs make norfen faster.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Cardiac valvulopathy and primary pulmonary hypertension on chronic dosing — basis for 1997 market withdrawal

notes: Fenfluramine itself is a relatively safe SERT releaser; the danger is its metabolite norfenfluramine, which is a potent 5-HT2B agonist (Ki 52 nM, EC50 ~18 nM, Emax ~73%). After 24+ months chronic dosing ~30% of patients develop echocardiographic valvulopathy. Reformulated as Fintepla for Dravet syndrome 2020 at sub-anorectic doses with REMS.

name: Fenethylline

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Codrug: hepatic metabolism cleaves the ethyltheophylline linker to yield ~24.5% amphetamine + ~13.7% theophylline (oral dose). The amphetamine produces classic DA/NE release; theophylline blocks adenosine A1/A2A receptors, adding alertness without the typical sympathomimetic anxiety. The combination is reported subjectively as 'smoother' than amphetamine alone.

routes.notes: Katselou 2016 — fenethylline oral, parent t1/2 short (~8 h); amphetamine and theophylline metabolites detected for 24+ h

notes: The famous 'Captagon' drug widely used in Middle East. Functionally an amphetamine + theophylline prodrug.

name: Benzphetamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Prodrug — undergoes N-debenzylation by CYP2B6 and CYP3A4 to dextromethamphetamine (and onward to d-amphetamine via N-demethylation). The intact benzphetamine is minimally pharmacologically active.

routes.notes: Parent t1/2 4–6 h; metabolites (d-meth, d-amph) drive duration and effect

notes: FDA-approved Schedule III anorectic. Prodrug of d-methamphetamine and d-amphetamine. Triggers positive amphetamine UDS.

name: Phentermine

binding.notes: Critically, phentermine is INACTIVE as a ligand or agonist of 5-HT2 receptors — this is why phen-only had no valvulopathy/PPH signal while fenfluramine did

functional.notes: Rothman/Baumann 2003 — phentermine is NE-selective releaser
Weak SERT releaser — clinically negligible

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: NE/DA release without significant SERT engagement; α,α-dimethyl substitution protects from MAO and CYP and gives long half-life (~20 h).

routes.notes: FDA label / DrugBank — Cmax ~200 ng/mL at 15 mg steady state, Tmax 6 h, t1/2 20–25 h (pH-dependent; 7–8 h in acidic urine). Only ~6% metabolised; mostly excreted unchanged renally.

notes: Currently FDA-approved as Adipex-P (15/37.5 mg) and Qsymia (phentermine + topiramate). The α,α-dimethyl gives long t1/2 and pure NE-DA release without 5-HT2B activity → no valvulopathy.

name: Phentermine+Fenfluramine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Combination: phentermine provides NE/DA stimulation + anorexia; fenfluramine provides SERT release / satiety. Synergistic weight loss but fenfluramine's norfenfluramine metabolite caused valvulopathy in ~30% of long-term users; combination withdrawn 1997. Phentermine alone has no valvulopathic signal because it has no 5-HT2B activity.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Valvulopathy 30%, PPH 23-fold relative risk — basis for 1997 withdrawal

notes: Historic combination, withdrawn 1997. See individual Phentermine and Fenfluramine records.

name: (+)-ephedrine

functional.notes: (+)-ephedrine substantially weaker than (-)-ephedrine (43-72 nM); the (-) form is the clinical/natural enantiomer

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Indirect sympathomimetic via NE release; β-hydroxyl reduces CNS penetration ~10× vs amphetamine. Also has weak direct α/β agonism.

notes: The (+) enantiomer; weaker than natural (-)-ephedrine. Stereochemistry matters: ephedrine = erythro, pseudoephedrine = threo.

name: Ephedrine

functional.notes: (-)-ephedrine — 3× more potent than (+)-ephedrine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Indirect sympathomimetic (NE release) + weak direct α/β agonism. β-hydroxyl reduces BBB penetration; ephedrine is more peripheral than amphetamine.

routes.notes: Oral F 88%; ~60% renal excretion unchanged; t1/2 ~6 h (pH-dependent)

notes: Natural ephedrine from Ephedra sinica. Classic indirect sympathomimetic. β-hydroxyl differentiates it from amphetamine — less CNS stimulant, more peripheral pressor.

name: Pseudoephedrine

functional.notes: Modest NE release; 9-fold selectivity over DA

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Indirect sympathomimetic, almost entirely via NE release. Direct α1/α2/β receptor binding is negligible (Kact >10 µM). The diastereomer of ephedrine — threo configuration weakens NE release ~3× vs ephedrine.

routes.notes: F ~100%, Tmax 1–4 h (IR) / 2–6 h (ER), t1/2 5.4 h (range 3–16 h pH-dependent); 43–96% renal excretion unchanged

notes: The threo-diastereomer of ephedrine. Far weaker CNS effect than ephedrine despite similar pressor activity. Used as nasal decongestant.

name: (−)-pseudoephedrine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: The (-) enantiomer of pseudoephedrine — opposite stereochemistry to OTC Sudafed. Pharmacologically weaker than (+); not used clinically.

notes: Mirror image of OTC pseudoephedrine. Limited published data; assumed weaker NE release.

name: 2-(methylamine)-1-phenyl-1-propanol

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Racemic ephedrine — see (+)-ephedrine and Ephedrine records.

notes: Racemic. Pharmacology = weighted mix of (-) and (+) ephedrine.

name: Aminorex

functional.notes: Notable SERT release component — distinguishes aminorex from amphetamine and explains the PPH risk
Weak direct 5-HT2B agonism (33× weaker than its NE release EC50). PPH mechanism likely also via SERT-released 5-HT acting at vascular 5-HT2B.

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Mixed monoamine releaser with significant SERT component → indirect 5-HT2B activation on pulmonary vasculature → mitogenesis → PPH. Caused epidemic of 582 PPH cases 1965–1972 (Gurtner BMJ doi:10.1136/bmj.4.5680.279).

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Primary pulmonary hypertension — caused European PPH epidemic 1965–1972 (582 cases), withdrawn

notes: First synthetic anorectic to cause an epidemic of PPH — established the 5-HT2B/SERT-release link to pulmonary vascular disease. Withdrawn 1972.

name: 4-methylaminorex

functional.notes: Brandt 2014 — cis-4-MAR is among the most potent DA releasers known
Modest SERT release — concerning for 5-HT2B liability

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Extremely potent monoamine releaser; cis-(±) is recreational form. Stereochemistry critical — trans isomers much weaker.

routes.notes: User reports 12–16 h duration oral; t1/2 estimated ~10–19 h

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Davis & Brewster 1988 fatal hepatic necrosis case (PMID 3373171)

notes: Long-acting, extremely potent — among the most potent DA releasers documented. Cis-(±)-4-MAR is the recreational stereoisomer.

name: 3-Methylaminorex

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Regioisomer of 4-MAR with the methyl on the oxazoline ring nitrogen rather than C4. Limited published binding data; expected weaker than 4-MAR.

notes: Less studied than 4-MAR. Aminorex congener.

name: 4,4'-Dimethylaminorex

binding.notes: Maier 2018 — 4,4'-DMAR is inactive at 5-HT2B despite being a balanced SNDRA

functional.notes: Well-balanced SERT release — comparable potency to DA and NE; closer to MDMA than amphetamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Balanced triple monoamine releaser (DA ≈ NE ≈ 5-HT all in 8–27 nM range) → high serotonin syndrome risk in OD especially with co-ingestants. Despite SERT release, no direct 5-HT2B activity.

notes: Caused ≥31 deaths in Europe by Feb 2014 (Brandt 2014). Balanced SNDRA → hyperthermic serotonin syndrome. Often co-ingested with other stimulants which amplified toxicity.

name: 4'-Fluoro-4-methylaminorex

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Fluorinated 4-MAR analogue; expected potent monoamine releaser like parent.

notes: Research chemical aminorex congener.

name: 4′-Chloro-4-methylaminorex

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Chlorinated 4-MAR analogue; para-chloro likely shifts to SERT-heavy profile.

notes: Research chemical aminorex congener.

name: 4B-MAR

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Brominated 4-MAR analogue; SERT-shifted by para-bromo.

notes: Research chemical aminorex congener.

name: Fluminorex

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Trifluoromethyl aminorex analogue developed as anorectic. Limited published data.

notes: Aminorex analogue, abandoned anorectic.

name: Methedrone

functional.notes: SERT-preferring; β-keto + para-methoxy combination shifts to serotonergic

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: β-keto analogue of PMMA. SERT-dominant releaser → serotonin syndrome risk. Lack of DA component → users keep redosing seeking effect → hyperthermic toxicity. Multiple Swedish fatalities (Wikström 2010).

routes.notes: Reported t1/2 ~26 h — unusually long for a cathinone

notes: β-keto cathinone with para-methoxy. Caused fatal serotonin-syndrome poisonings in Sweden 2010. Note: belongs to cathinone group, may be better categorised there.

name: Pemoline

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Mechanism distinct from amphetamines — primarily dopamine reuptake inhibition with mild releasing component, NO significant noradrenergic effect (PMID 9708845). Lack of peripheral sympathomimetic side effects but produces dopamine-mediated alerting.

routes.notes: t1/2 7–12 h (7 h children, 11–12 h adults); enables once-daily dosing

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Idiosyncratic fatal hepatic failure — 21+ documented cases, 13 deaths/transplants — withdrawn from US market 2005 (FDA black box 1999)

notes: Withdrawn in US 2005 due to fatal idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity. Mechanism is selective DA release/reuptake inhibition without NE component.

name: Cyclazodone

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Pemoline analogue with cyclopropyl-amino substitution; CNS stimulant of the oxazoline class. Limited published mechanistic data.

notes: Related to pemoline. Sold as designer 'nootropic' research chemical.

name: Propylhexedrine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Cyclohexyl analogue of methamphetamine — saturated ring loses TAAR1 efficacy and reduces CNS penetration vs methamphetamine. Primarily peripheral sympathomimetic; nasal decongestant via NE release / α1 agonism.

notes: OTC Benzedrex inhaler. Widely abused via oral/IV ingestion despite intended inhalational use (cardiotoxicity risk).

name: Dmaa

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Non-aromatic aliphatic amine NDRA — releases NE and DA without aromatic ring. Indirectly raises blood pressure via NE release. Lacks TAAR1 efficacy. Recently confirmed as NDRA by Small 2023 (doi:10.1124/jpet.122.001514).

routes.notes: t1/2 ~8.5 h — accumulates with repeated dosing

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Severe hypertension, cerebral haemorrhage, MI — ≥5 deaths attributed; banned by FDA from supplements 2013

notes: Aliphatic NDRA. Was marketed as supplement (Jack3D, OxyElitePro) until FDA banned 2013 after deaths.

name: DMHA

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Aliphatic amine NDRA similar to DMAA; sold as DMAA replacement in supplements after 2013 ban. Mechanism presumed NE/DA release; limited published data.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Hypertension, tachycardia; banned in some markets

notes: DMAA replacement marketed in supplements. Similar mechanism, limited data.

name: Phenethylamine

functional.notes: Bunzow/Borowsky 2001 — PEA is the prototypical TAAR1 endogenous agonist

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Endogenous trace amine; equipotent to amphetamine at DAT in vitro but orally inactive in humans up to 1.6 g (Sabelli 1986) due to rapid first-pass MAO metabolism.

routes.notes: Endogenous PEA t1/2 ~30 s in DA neurons; oral PEA t1/2 5–10 min (intestinal + hepatic MAO). Effectively orally inactive.

notes: The endogenous trace amine prototype. α-methylation (→ amphetamine) protects from MAO and gives oral activity.

name: PEA

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See Phenethylamine record.

notes: Duplicate of Phenethylamine.

name: N-methylphenethylamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Endogenous trace amine; human TAAR1 agonist. Preferentially metabolised by MAO-B (KM 4.13 µM) vs MAO-A (KM 58.8 µM). Pressor activity ~1/350 of epinephrine.

notes: Endogenous trace amine present in human brain. MAO-B preferred substrate; orally weak.

name: N-Ethylphenethylamine hydrochloride

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-ethyl PEA; reduced TAAR1 efficacy and increased MAO resistance vs PEA. Rapidly metabolised; orally weak.

notes: N-ethyl trace amine; minor pharmacology.

name: Tyramine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Endogenous trace amine, TAAR1 agonist, indirect sympathomimetic via VMAT2 displacement. Does NOT cross BBB — pharmacologic effects entirely peripheral. The 'cheese reaction': MAOI inhibition allows oral tyramine to escape first-pass MAO → massive peripheral NE release from sympathetic terminals → hypertensive crisis.

routes.notes: Almost entirely degraded by intestinal/hepatic MAO-A; threshold for cheese reaction on MAOI is ~10 mg

drug_interactions_pk.mechanism: intestinal MAO-A inhibition + hepatic MAO-A inhibition = absent first-pass degradation
drug_interactions_pk.clinical_effect: Hypertensive crisis ('cheese reaction'): 10 mg dietary tyramine causes severe BP spike, 25 mg can be lethal in MAOI users

notes: Major dietary amine in aged cheese, cured meat, fermented foods. Cheese reaction is the canonical MAOI dietary interaction.

name: tyramine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See Tyramine record.

notes: Duplicate of Tyramine.

name: m-tyramine

functional.notes: Slightly more potent than p-tyramine at hTAAR1

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Endogenous trace amine; similar profile to p-tyramine.

notes: Endogenous trace amine, less studied than p-tyramine.

name: octopamine

functional.notes: One of four endogenous TAAR1 agonists (PEA, tyramine, octopamine, synephrine)

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Endogenous trace amine; 400–2000× weaker than NE at mammalian adrenergic receptors. Does not cross BBB readily.

notes: Endogenous trace amine. Major neurotransmitter in invertebrates (analogue of NE in insects).

name: (-)-octopamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See octopamine record.

notes: Duplicate.

name: oxedrine

functional.notes: Low-potency TAAR1 partial agonist

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Weak α1-selective adrenergic agonist + low-potency TAAR1 agonist. p-Synephrine (Citrus aurantium) — distinct from m-synephrine (phenylephrine) which is ~100× more potent at α1.

notes: Found in bitter orange (Citrus aurantium); common in fat-burner supplements. Very weak compared to m-synephrine (phenylephrine).

name: (+)-oxedrine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: S-(+)-synephrine; weaker enantiomer.

notes: Enantiomer of synephrine.

name: (-)-oxedrine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: R-(-)-synephrine; the more α1-active enantiomer.

notes: Enantiomer of synephrine.

name: D-synephrine(1+)

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Protonated form of D-synephrine; same pharmacology as parent.

notes: Ionic form of D-synephrine.

name: phenylephrine

binding.notes: Selective α1 full agonist; minimal β activity

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Direct α1 agonist (Gq → PLC → IP3/DAG → vasoconstriction). The meta-hydroxyl positions it for α1 selectivity unlike para (synephrine) which is weak.

routes.notes: Hatton 2007 meta-analysis — oral F is essentially zero (massive first-pass MAO-A); explains FDA 2023 finding that oral phenylephrine is ineffective as decongestant
IV phenylephrine is the standard pressor for spinal anaesthesia hypotension

notes: FDA advisory panel September 2023 found oral phenylephrine ineffective as nasal decongestant — massive first-pass metabolism leaves no systemic drug. IV is potent and effective.

name: Hordenine

functional.notes: Bunzow 2001 — hordenine at 1 µM matches PEA at 1 µM in stimulating cAMP

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Indirect sympathomimetic via NE release; selective MAO-B substrate (Km 479 µM, Vmax 128 nM/mg/h in rat liver, not deaminated by MAO-A). Poor BBB penetration — peripheral activity dominates.

notes: Found in barley and some cacti. Marketed in pre-workout supplements as 'focus' ingredient. Poor BBB penetration limits CNS effect.

name: hordenine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See Hordenine record.

notes: Duplicate of Hordenine.

name: N-methyltyramine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Trace amine, TAAR1 agonist. Releases NE indirectly; poor BBB penetration.

notes: Endogenous trace amine; found in some cacti and bitter orange. Pre-workout supplement ingredient.

name: dopamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Endogenous catecholamine. Full agonist at all five DA receptor subtypes; at high doses also activates α1 and β1 directly. Does NOT cross BBB.

routes.notes: Plasma t1/2 ~1 min (newborn ~2 min, preterm ~5 min); rapidly metabolised by MAO + COMT + ALDH to HVA

notes: Endogenous neurotransmitter. Used clinically as IV pressor (peripherally) — does not cross BBB so no CNS effects of exogenous administration.

name: 3-Hydroxytyramine hydrobromide

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Salt form of dopamine.

notes: Salt form of dopamine. See dopamine record.

name: deoxyepinephrine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: N-methyldopamine; partial agonist at DA and adrenergic receptors. Active metabolite of ibopamine. Does cross BBB to a limited extent.

notes: Active metabolite of ibopamine (oral DA prodrug). Used historically for cardiac inotropy.

name: oxidopamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Selectively taken up by DAT and NET into catecholaminergic neurons where auto-oxidation generates ROS → mitochondrial dysfunction → selective DA/NE neuron death. Standard research lesioning agent for Parkinson's disease models.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Selective dopaminergic neurotoxicity — research-only, not for human use

notes: 6-OHDA is the classic experimental neurotoxin for selective DA terminal lesions. Standard tool in Parkinson's disease animal models.

name: 5-Hydroxydopamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Like 6-OHDA but more NET-selective; used for noradrenergic lesioning.

notes: Noradrenergic neurotoxin counterpart to 6-OHDA.

name: 3-O-methyldopamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: COMT metabolite of dopamine. Endogenous trace amine. TAAR1 partial agonist.

notes: Endogenous metabolite of dopamine via COMT.

name: 4-O-methyldopamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Regioisomer of 3-O-methyldopamine; weak TAAR1 agonist.

notes: Catechol O-methylation product (minor pathway).

name: 4-Fluorodeprenyl

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Propargylamine MAO-B inhibitor like selegiline. Fluorination at para position alters CYP metabolism — slower N-dealkylation to amphetamine metabolites; potentially safer profile. Used as PET tracer ([18F]-4-F-deprenyl) for in vivo MAO-B imaging.

notes: Selegiline analogue used as PET imaging agent. Reduced amphetamine metabolite formation vs parent selegiline.

name: DESOXY

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Note: DESOXY in PIHKAL is actually 4-methyl-2,5-dimethoxyamphetamine (DESOXY-DOM); separate from desoxypipradrol. As PIHKAL DESOXY (Shulgin entry #61): structural analogue lacking the 5-methoxy of DOM. Limited published pharmacology.

data_gaps_remaining: Identity ambiguous in source; no published EC50
notes: Name DESOXY ambiguous: PIHKAL entry vs desoxypipradrol; assuming PIHKAL DOM analogue.

name: 2-methylamphetamine

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Ring-methylated amphetamine; ortho-methyl is sterically tolerated, profile similar to amphetamine with possible slight DA shift. Limited published data.

notes: Research chemical; very limited data.

name: 3-CAF

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Meta-chloro is less SERT-shifted than para-chloro (which is PCA, a serotonergic neurotoxin). Limited published data on m-CA specifically.

notes: Meta-chloroamphetamine. Distinct from PCA — less serotonergic shift expected. Research chemical.

name: Methedrone

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See Methedrone (lowercased) record above.

notes: Capitalisation duplicate.

name: Mescaline

binding.notes: Range across labs Ki 550–17,400 nM, EC50 88–30,200 nM, Emax 33–107%

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Classical psychedelic. 5-HT2A partial agonist with significant biased agonism at 5-HT2C. NOT amphetamine-like despite having an aminoethyl side chain (no α-methyl).

routes.notes: Recent re-analysis (2020s) gives t1/2 ~3.6 h (range 2.6–5.3 h), correcting earlier 6 h estimate. Onset 0.5–0.9 h; Tmax 1.6–2.3 h.

metabolism.notes: Mescaline is a poor substrate of purified human MAO; deamination pathway unclear. Not significantly metabolised by CYP2D6.

notes: Mescaline is a phenethylamine but a classical psychedelic, not a stimulant — included here because of phenethylamine class membership. Active metabolite of peyote (Lophophora williamsii).

name: 2C-B

binding.notes: Concerning 5-HT2B activity (Ki 13.5–97 nM) — chronic 2C-B use may carry valvulopathy risk

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: Classical 5-HT2A partial agonist psychedelic. Notable 5-HT2B activity is a chronic-use concern.

notes: Classical 2C psychedelic. Note: not a stimulant per se but included due to phenethylamine class membership.

name: 25T-NBOMe

binding.notes: Estimated based on the NBOMe series boost: parent 2C-T is moderate, N-benzyl modification increases affinity 30–100×

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: NBOMe family — extreme 5-HT2A agonism with very narrow therapeutic index; 5-HT2B activity adds cardiotoxicity risk.

off_targets.clinical_consequence: Cardiotoxicity / valvulopathy potential; multiple NBOMe deaths reported

data_gaps_remaining: Specific Ki for 25T-NBOMe family members not individually published
notes: NBOMe variant. NBOMe N-benzyl modification boosts 5-HT2A affinity 30–100× over parent 2C compound. Multiple deaths in series.

name: 2C-T-4-NBOMe

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See 25T-NBOMe record.

notes: NBOMe variant of 2C-T-4.

name: 2C-T-7-NBOMe

pharmacology.downstream_signalling: See 25T-NBOMe record. NBOMe of 2C-T-7.

notes: NBOMe variant of 2C-T-7.
